Banxico interest rate differential; strong policy framework; recovery in remittances and tourism","outcome":"Peso was one of the better-performing currencies; remained stable despite implied capital outflows","dates":["June 2021 - June 2022"],"quantities":["8 percent dollar index appreciation"],"excerpt":"Despite the continued reduction in holdings of local-currency debt by foreigners over the past year, the peso has performed well, especially compared to other emerging market currencies.","locator":"page 71","attribution":"International Monetary Fund","period_fit":"Mid-2021 to mid-2022 review period; peso stability narrative consistent with this timeframe","source_limitations":["Correlation analysis rather than causal attribution; carry trade explanation not fully validated; IMF staff calculations based on Bloomberg data"],"question_ids":["5B.3","5B.9","5B.10"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[]},{"draft_id":"D0002","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Banxico responded quickly to rising inflation pressures, pushing the interest rate spread versus the U.S. to over 6 percent, close to previous highs in the past decade, making Mexico attractive for carry trades.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Banxico (Banco de México)","action":"raised policy interest rate to create large spread vs U.S.","mechanism":"Interest rate differential creating carry trade attractiveness","outcome":"Mexico had high ratio of carry to implied volatility; peso attracted carry trade support","dates":[],"quantities":["over 6 percent interest rate spread vs U.S."],"excerpt":"Banxico's quick response to rising inflation pressures pushed the interest rate spread versus the U.S. to over 6 percent, close to previous highs in the past decade or so.","locator":"page 71","attribution":"International Monetary Fund","period_fit":"Mid-2021 to mid-2022; consistent with inflation surge period","source_limitations":["Claim about attractiveness based on quantitative metric but correlation between carry ratio and currency performance noted as weak"],"question_ids":["5B.3","5B.9"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[]},{"draft_id":"D0003","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Pension funds in Mexico became the biggest holders of domestic government securities in mid-2020, with projected annual purchases of roughly USD 7-10 billion even if assets remained at 20 percent of GDP, matching peak foreign sales recorded in the last ten years.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican pension funds (AFOREs)","action":"accumulated domestic government securities, becoming largest holders","mechanism":"pension reform increasing contributions; domestic investor substitution for foreigners","outcome":"Pension funds became biggest holders by mid-2020; projected annual purchases of USD 7-10 billion can match highest foreign annual sales","dates":["mid-2020 (holdings); projected forward"],"quantities":["USD 7-10 billion annual purchases","20 percent of GDP assets"],"excerpt":"Pension funds in particular have been buying domestic government securities and became the biggest holders in mid-2020.","locator":"page 72","attribution":"International Monetary Fund","period_fit":"Mid-2020 to forward projections; where actual exceeds shadow price, excise rate reduced","outcome":"Formal fiscal rule governing fuel pricing; subsidies decline when market prices fall; methodology enshrined in Presidential decree","dates":["methodology established December 2019"],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Shadow prices are constructed using four components. First, a base price component is set at the fuel price as of November 2018, uprated with inflation every 15 days. A second component is a reference price that tracks contemporaneous trends in commodity markets - this is based on the U.S. Gulf Coast waterborne ticker.","locator":"page 74","attribution":"International Monetary Fund","period_fit":"Methodology established December 2019; operational during 2022 fuel price surge; expected to continue 2023","source_limitations":["Formula details from government decree; effectiveness during extreme price volatility not fully demonstrated in excerpt"],"question_ids":["5B.3","5B.4"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[]},{"draft_id":"D0005","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Fuel subsidies peaked in June 2022, reducing retail fuel prices by as much as 30 percent, directly reducing headline inflation by about two percentage points when it would have peaked at nearly 10 percent.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican government","action":"implemented fuel subsidies to contain inflation","mechanism":"Fuel subsidies reducing domestic retail prices despite global price increases following Russia's invasion of Ukraine","outcome":"Direct effect of fuel subsidy reduced headline inflation by approximately 2 percentage points; without subsidy inflation would have peaked near 10%","dates":["June 2022 (peak subsidy)"],"quantities":["30 percent price reduction; 2 percentage point inflation reduction; ~10% would-be peak inflation","6 percent of consumption basket (fuel weight)"],"excerpt":"Peaking in June, subsidies reduced prices by as much as 30 percent. With fuel at about 6 percent of the consumption basket, the direct effects of the fuel subsidy reduced headline inflation by about two percentage points, when it would have peaked at nearly 10 percent.","locator":"page 74","attribution":"International Monetary Fund","period_fit":"2022 inflation surge period; directly relevant to shock response assessment","source_limitations":["May understate total impact due to second-round effects (distribution costs, transport) not fully captured","verification_notes":["IMF staff calculations; direct effect only, second-round effects not quantified"]}],"verification_status":"pending"},{"draft_id":"D0006","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"While domestic fuel subsidies cost MEX$395.4 billion (1.4% of GDP), windfall oil revenues of MEX$397.8 billion roughly matched this cost, suggesting the subsidy scheme was approximately self-financed through oil export gains in 2022.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"mixed","actor":"Mexican government","action":"subsidized fuel while benefiting from oil export windfall","mechanism":"Oil revenue gains from export price increases offset domestic fuel subsidy costs","outcome":"Net fiscal cost of fuel subsidies approximately zero when accounting from oil revenue gains relative to 2022 budget","dates":[],"quantities":["MEX$395.4 billion fuel subsidy cost","MEX$397.8 billion oil revenue windfall gain","1.4% of GDP (subsidy)"],"excerpt":"While domestic fuel subsidies are expected to cost MEX$395.4 billion, the windfall gain in oil revenues relative to the 2022 budget approved in 2021 is estimated at MEX$397.8 billion, suggesting that exports can cover the costs of the subsidy scheme.","locator":"page 74","attribution":"International Monetary Fund","period_fit":"2022; budget vs. actual oil revenue comparison","source_limitations":["Risk noted if crack spread (refining margin) increases sharply; subsidy could exceed revenue gain in that scenario","verification_notes":["SHCP estimated figures"]},{"draft_id":"D0007","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Rural poverty showed modest improvement from 57.7% in 2018 to 56.8% by end of 2020, while urban poverty worsened from 36.8% to 40.1% over the same period, with urban deterioration linked to illness and public health restrictions during the pandemic.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Mexican households","action":"experienced divergent poverty trends by geography during pandemic","mechanism":"Pandemic illness and public health restrictions affected urban economic conditions","outcome":"Rural poverty improved modestly; urban poverty increased significantly; overall mixed poverty trajectory","dates":["2018 baseline; end of 2020 measurement"],"quantities":["57.7% to 56.8% rural (poverty and extreme poverty)","36.8% to 40.1% urban households in poverty"],"excerpt":"By the end of 2020, rural poverty had posted a modest improvement, with around 56.8 percent of the rural population in poverty or extreme poverty compared to 57.7 percent in 2018. However, the same period also saw a deterioration of conditions in urban areas, with around 40.1 percent of urban households estimated to be in some form of poverty—up from 36.8 percent in 2018—as illness and public health restrictions affected the economy.","locator":"page 73","attribution":"CONEVAL, 2022; IMF staff calculations","period_fit":"2018-2020 period; pandemic impact divergence between rural and urban","source_limitations":["CONEVAL official measurement; pandemic year data collection disruptions may affect precision"],"question_ids":["5B.1","5B.8"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[]},{"draft_id":"D0008","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexican government launched PACIC anti-inflation package in May 2022 costing MEX$541.2 billion (1.86% of GDP) including fuel subsidies (MEX$395.4bn/1.36% GDP), electricity subsidy (MEX$73bn/0.25% GDP), and food price measures (MEX$72.8bn/0.25% GDP).","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican government (SHCP)","action":"launched comprehensive anti-inflation package including fuel subsidies, electricity subsidy, and food price support programs","mechanism":"Direct subsidies (fuel, electricity); agricultural support programs (Sembrando Vida, Producción para el Bienestar, fertilizer, milk subsidy, rural supply); retail price agreement; tariff reduction","outcome":"Total fiscal cost of 1.86% of GDP for anti-inflation measures in 2022","dates":["May 2022 (PACIC launch)"],"quantities":["MEX$541.2 billion total (1.86% GDP)","MEX$395.4 billion fuel subsidy (1.36% GDP)","MEX$73 billion electricity subsidy (0.25% GDP)","MEX$72.8 billion food measures (0.25% GDP)"],"excerpt":"Total 541,223 1.86","locator":"page 74","attribution":"SHCP (Mexican Ministry of Finance)","period_fit":"2022 anti-inflation response; fiscal year 2022","source_limitations":["Budgetary costs as estimated by SHCP; actual may vary","verification_notes":["Budgetary cost breakdown by SHCP; includes both fuel subsidies and food price stabilization measures"]},{"draft_id":"D0009","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"The Mexican government reached agreement with major retailers to restrain price increases for 24 staple goods for six months with no fiscal or regulatory implications for the government, costing approximately MEX$1.2 billion in 2022 tariff revenue foregone for broader tariff reduction on 21 basic goods and 5 inputs.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican government and major retailers","action":"agreed to limit price increases on 24 staple goods; reduced import tariffs on basic goods and food production inputs","mechanism":"Voluntary retail price restraint agreement; tariff reduction on imports of 21 basic goods and 5 food production inputs","outcome":"Price restraint on staple goods at no direct fiscal cost; tariff reduction cost of MEX$1.2 billion in 2022","dates":["May 2022 (agreement)"],"quantities":["24 core food items price restraint","21 basic goods and 5 inputs covered by tariff reduction","MEX$1.2 billion tariff revenue foregone"],"excerpt":"The President announced that a number of major retailers in Mexico had agreed to restrain price increases for 24 staple goods initially for six months with no fiscal or regulatory implications for the government.","locator":"page 75","attribution":"International Monetary Fund","period_fit":"2022 anti-inflation measures; May 2022 onward","source_limitations":["Voluntary agreement with unclear enforcement mechanism; impact not clearly assessed in report","verification_notes":["Policy impact described as unclear"]},{"draft_id":"D0010","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Remittances to Mexico were countercyclical, increasing during both the Global Financial Crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic, driven by dollar appreciation boosting peso value of transfers and support efforts for relatives in Mexico.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican workers in the U.S.","action":"sent increased remittances to Mexico during U.S. economic downturns","mechanism":"Dollar appreciation during GFC increased peso value of dollar transfers; pandemic period saw efforts to support relatives","outcome":"Countercyclical flow provided economic support during U.S. downturns; remittances grew from under 1% of GDP in 2000 to nearly 4% of GDP by 2021","dates":["GFC (2008-2009); COVID-19 pandemic (2020-2021)","2000 to 2021 (structural growth)"],"quantities":["under 1% of GDP (2000)","nearly 4% of GDP (2021)"],"excerpt":"Remittances seem to be countercyclical; they were increasing in both the GFC and the COVID-19 pandemic.","locator":"page 76","attribution":"International Monetary Fund","period_fit":"GFC (2008-2009), COVID-19 (2020-2021), and structural growth 2000-2021","source_limitations":["COVID-19 period increase may partly reflect replacement of cash transfers by observable wire transfers","verification_notes":["U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, INEGI, Banxico data"]},{"draft_id":"D0011","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico's economic integration with the U.S. has made the Mexican business cycle increasingly correlated with U.S. fluctuations: a 1% change in U.S. GDP was associated with 1.5% change in Mexico GDP in the 2010s versus 0.2% in the 1980s, with manufacturing (80% automotive) driving three-fourths of short-term GDP fluctuations.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"context","actor":"Mexican economy","action":"became increasingly integrated with and sensitive to U.S. business cycle","mechanism":"Trade channel: manufacturing sector (one-fifth of GDP, 80% automotive) explains three-fourths of short-term GDP fluctuations; one-to-one short-term association between Mexico manufacturing exports and U.S. production","outcome":"High economic sensitivity to U.S. fluctuations; structural vulnerability to external demand shocks","dates":["NAFTA mid-1990s onward; 1980s vs 2010s comparison"],"quantities":["1.5% Mexico GDP change per 1% U.S. GDP change (2010s)","0.2% in 1980s","three-fourths of short-term GDP fluctuations from manufacturing","one-fifth of GDP in manufacturing","80% foreign demand share in automotive"],"excerpt":"A one-percent change in U.S. GDP was associated with a 1.5 percent change in Mexico GDP in the 2010s, compared to about 0.2 percent in the 1980s.","locator":"page 76","attribution":"International Monetary Fund","period_fit":"NAFTA period (mid-1990s onward); rolling regression analysis 1980s-2010s","source_limitations":["12-year rolling window regression; correlation does not imply causation for policy purposes","verification_notes":["U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, INEGI; Fund staff calculations"]},{"draft_id":"D0012","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Food prices contributed roughly half of the increase in Mexico's inflation above Banxico's upper target limit, consistent with historical patterns since the 2001 adoption of inflation targeting, with past above-target food episodes occurring in 2008, 2011-13, and 2017-18.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Global and Mexican food markets","action":"drove food price inflation disproportionately compared to other components","mechanism":"Food price shocks; structural factors making food more prominent in Mexico's inflation basket","outcome":"Food inflation was primary driver of above-target headline inflation; contributing roughly half of the overshoot","dates":["2021-2022 inflation surge; historical episodes in 2008, 2011-13, 2017-18"],"quantities":["roughly half of inflation above upper target limit (food contribution)"],"excerpt":"An important difference is the greater role of food prices in the inflation surge in Mexico, contributing roughly half of the increase in inflation above the upper limit of Banxico's inflation target range.","locator":"page 80","attribution":"International Monetary Fund","period_fit":"2021-2022 inflation surge; historical context since inflation targeting adoption 2001","source_limitations":["IMF staff characterization; underlying food price dynamics not fully explained in excerpt","verification_notes":["Haver Analytics data;
